✓ProvaLivre

Personalized, anti-cheating exams for underfunded public schools

A teacher turns their own lecture material into a reusable question bank, then generates a different exam for every student — same difficulty, different questions and numbers — with answer keys computed by code and verified by a human.

Author: Carine Zambrano  ·  Course: MGT 409
GitHub: github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/provalivre  (replace with your repo URL)
App: runs locally — python app.py → http://127.0.0.1:5000

1. Motivation

My uncle, Erick, teaches civil engineering at a public technical high school in Brazil. His school is chronically underfunded, and like most public-school teachers he carries a heavy load with almost no tooling budget. His single biggest assessment headache is cheating.

In his classroom, students copy from one another during exams — a practice so common it has a name, “filar.” One student solves a question and the answer travels down the row; worse, the same exam is reused across terms, so answers get memorized and passed to the next year's class. His current options are all bad:

  • One exam for everyone — trivial to copy from a neighbor.
  • Hand-made variants — he writes exercise lists with full worked solutions by hand, which he described as “trabalho da gota serena” (grinding, endless work). Making a genuinely different exam for each of 30–40 students is simply not feasible by hand.
“Keep a bank of, say, 50 questions. Each student's exam pulls 10 at random, so the difficulty is the same but every exam is different — so they can't copy. For multiple choice, shuffle the answer options too. For the math questions, keep the same formula but change the input values so the answers differ. That last part is more complex — I don't know how to do it.”
— Erick, translated from his voice messages describing what he needs

The cost. A teacher spends hours per exam hand-building questions and keys; the payoff is undermined the moment students copy. Erick asked for exactly one thing: a way to give every student a fair, different exam without doubling his workload. That request defined this project.

2. What is new

Plenty of tools touch pieces of this problem; none solve Erick's version of it.

Existing optionWhat it doesWhy it falls short here
LMS (Canvas, Google Classroom, Moodle)Hosts materials, collects submissionsNo exam generation; no anti-cheat question variants
Quiz tools (Google Forms, Quizizz, Kahoot)Shuffle question/option orderShuffle order only — same questions and same numbers for everyone
ChatGPTDrafts questions on requestNo persistent bank, no guaranteed-correct math, no per-student assembly, no verification workflow
Publisher test banks / ExamSoftLarge pre-built item poolsCostly, English-only, generic — not built from the teacher's own Portuguese material

What ProvaLivre does differently:

  1. Builds a bank from the teacher's own lecture material, in Portuguese, tagged by concept and difficulty.
  2. Generates a unique exam per student: random question selection to a chosen difficulty mix, shuffled order, shuffled multiple-choice options, and numeric questions whose numbers change per student.
  3. For math, the AI writes a parameterized template; Python computes the answer, so the answer key is always arithmetically correct — this is the part Erick said he couldn't figure out.
  4. A human-in-the-loop gate: AI-written formulas must be verified by the teacher before any student sees them.
  5. Free, local, bilingual — designed for a school with no budget.
The twist that makes it more than a “question generator”: a code-verified numeric-variant engine plus a human-approval gate, so each student gets a mathematically-different-but-fair exam with a provably correct key.

3. The agents

ProvaLivre is a pipeline of four focused agents. The first three use the gpt-6-luna model (via Portkey — the course model, and a capable, inexpensive choice); the fourth uses no model at all.

Figure 1. Agent pipeline. The first three agents (gpt-6-luna) author questions once into a persistent bank; the deterministic Exam Assembler builds each student's unique exam from that bank at no token cost.
AgentJobTool it usesModel
Concept ExtractorPull teachable concepts from lecture textFile parser (PDF / PPTX / text)gpt-6-luna
Question AuthorWrite multiple-choice & short-answer questions per difficulty—gpt-6-luna
Math Variant BuilderWrite parameterized numeric templatesCode executor (verifies every formula)gpt-6-luna
Exam AssemblerBuild each student's unique exam + key— (deterministic)none

Why the split matters. The model only writes a math template and a formula; it never does arithmetic. The code executor runs the formula over sample values to confirm it computes, then the Exam Assembler plugs in each student's random numbers and computes the exact answer. The model is used for language, Python for arithmetic — playing to the strengths of each.

Cost per user, and at scale

The “unit” here is a teacher. A teacher builds a bank when they start a new unit — assume a generous 2 builds per month. Exams themselves are free.

ScenarioBank builds / moMonthly cost
1 teacher2$0.014
100 teachers200$1.40
10,000 teachers20,000$140

Ten thousand teachers — each giving every student a unique exam — for about $140/month.

Cost-reduction steps taken, and their trade-offs

  1. Deterministic assembly (biggest lever). A naive design would ask the model to generate each student's exam. At ~16k tokens per exam that is ~$0.007 per student — $70 for a 10,000-student cohort, every single exam. ProvaLivre authors once and recombines for free, driving per-exam cost to ~$0. Trade-off: none to quality — questions are still LLM-authored; assembly only selects, shuffles, and plugs in numbers.
  2. Batched authoring. Rather than one call per concept (~24 calls), the app makes one call per difficulty×type across all concepts (10 calls). Trade-off: slightly less per-concept depth; measured output quality remained high (see the generated questions above).
  3. Input cap (60,000 chars). Oversized uploads are truncated, bounding input tokens. Trade-off: very long documents are clipped; the cap is well above a normal lecture.
  4. Reusable persistent bank. Authoring cost is amortized across every student and every term the bank is reused.

5. Safety

ProvaLivre's inputs include untrusted files (anything a teacher uploads) and model output that ends up in front of students, so the risks are real:

  • Attacks. A malicious lecture file could try prompt injection (“ignore your instructions…”); a crafted formula could try to run code.
  • Malfunction. The model could invent a wrong formula or return malformed data — and a wrong answer key reaching students is a serious failure.
  • Overspending. A huge upload or a runaway request could drain the token budget.

Each risk has a built, tested defense. The app ships a one-click demonstration that runs them all; every check passes:

Figure 5. The built-in safety demonstration: all seven defenses pass, across attack, malfunction, and overspend categories.
RiskDefenseEvidence
Code injection via formulaFormulas are parsed with an AST whitelist; no imports, attribute access, or arbitrary calls__import__(...) → blocked
Prompt-injection / malformed outputUntrusted material is isolated in tags; every question is schema-validated and dropped if malformedBad MC question → rejected
Invented / wrong mathCode executor runs each formula before acceptance; bad templates rejectedDivide-by-zero template → rejected
Unverified AI arithmeticHuman-approval gate: AI math is withheld from exams until a teacher verifies a worked sampleUnapproved math → excluded from exam
OverspendingInput truncation (60k chars) + hard cap on questions per build120k chars → truncated; 150-question plan → refused
Why the human gate matters. Even though Python computes the arithmetic perfectly, the formula is AI-written and could be wrong. ProvaLivre never lets an unverified AI formula reach a student — the teacher sees a worked example (numbers → answer) and must click “Approve (I verified the math).”

6. Impact

The headline is time and fairness, measured against how Erick works today.

30unique exams in <1 min
$0.007cost for the whole class
0duplicate exams (of 30)

Time. Hand-building even a few genuine exam variants with worked keys takes hours; Erick does this every term. ProvaLivre produces 30 distinct exams and 30 answer keys in under a minute from a bank that itself took ~20 seconds and under a cent to build. Conservatively, that is several hours saved per exam cycle, repeated every unit. (Projection based on measured generation time; labeled as an estimate pending a classroom timing.)

Fairness & integrity. Copying from a neighbor stops working when the neighbor's exam has different questions, different option orders, and different numbers. Reuse across terms stops working when the bank reshuffles every time. This directly addresses the “filar” problem Erick described.

Reach. Because the marginal cost per student is ~$0, the same tool serves one classroom or an entire district for the price of a few coffees a month. The rubric notes that impact on classrooms counts as much as business savings — here the beneficiary is a public school with no budget.

Real-user voice. The entire design came from Erick's own description of his needs (quoted in §1). A live classroom pilot with his students is the planned next validation step; a short reaction from him is being collected and will be attached if received before submission.

7. Limits & next steps

  • Question review is partly manual. Math is gated behind human approval; multiple-choice and short-answer questions are schema-checked but their content still deserves a teacher's eye. A lightweight approve/edit flow for all types is the next step.
  • Worked step-by-step solutions. Erick wants students who miss a question to see a full worked solution. The app produces answer keys today; generating and showing step-by-step solutions is the top feature on the roadmap.
  • No student portal yet. The app is teacher-centric and export-based (printable exams + keys). Student logins and in-app delivery are future work.
  • Template vs. variant approval. A teacher approves a template; because every variant is computed by the same verified formula, the per-student numbers are safe once the template is approved.
  • Single subject tested. Built and measured on civil-engineering material; broadening to other subjects is straightforward but untested.

Bilingual by design. The whole interface toggles between Portuguese and English so Erick and an English-speaking reviewer can both use it:
